# The aged tumor microenvironment limits T cell control of cancer

## Abstract

The etiology and effect of age-related immune dysfunction in cancer is not completely understood. Here we show that limited priming of CD8+ T cells in the aged tumor microenvironment (TME) outweighs cell-intrinsic defects in limiting tumor control. Increased tumor growth in aging is associated with reduced CD8+ T cell infiltration and function. Transfer of T cells from young mice does not restore tumor control in aged mice owing to rapid induction of T cell dysfunction. Cell-extrinsic signals in the aged TME drive a tumor-infiltrating age-associated dysfunctional (TTAD) cell state that is functionally, transcriptionally and epigenetically distinct from canonical T cell exhaustion. Altered natural killer cell–dendritic cell–CD8+ T cell cross-talk in aged tumors impairs T cell priming by conventional type 1 dendritic cells and promotes TTAD cell formation. Aged mice are thereby unable to benefit from therapeutic tumor vaccination. Critically, myeloid-targeted therapy to reinvigorate conventional type 1 dendritic cells can improve tumor control and restore CD8+ T cell immunity in aging.

Aging is one of the biggest risk factors for cancer development1. The rise in cancer incidence in older populations is paralleled by a progressive decline in immune function, including within the CD8+ T cell compartment2. Despite the critical importance of CD8+ T cells for effective antitumor immunity3,4, the impact of age-related T cell dysregulation on tumor control and immunotherapy outcomes remains poorly understood.

Aging promotes cancer progression through a variety of mechanisms, including accumulated cellular damage, increased systemic inflammation and attenuated adaptive immunity1. Age-related defects in T cells include reduced naive T cell repertoire, telomere erosion, accumulated DNA damage and increased proinflammatory features5-7. However, the extent to which these changes contribute to impaired CD8+ T cell responses in aged tumors relative to age-independent mechanisms, such as the development of T cell exhaustion, remains unknown.

Largely driven by persistent stimulation of CD8+ T cells, exhausted CD8+ T cells portray a variety of functional defects, including loss of effector cytokine production and diminished cytotoxicity8-11. Prior work demonstrates that CD8+ T cell exhaustion is a fundamental dysfunctional state induced in many tumors and is not reversed by common therapeutic interventions11,12. Unfortunately, previous studies have been largely limited to the effects of aging in healthy donors6,13-15 or alternatively have focused on the impact of the tumor microenvironment (TME) alone in young mice. Therefore, the relative importance of age-associated CD8+ T cell dysfunction versus chronic stimulation-driven CD8+ T cell exhaustion in the aged TME remains unclear16.

Disentangling the influence of aging/senescence and exhaustion in mediating CD8+ T cell dysfunction within tumors is urgently needed to improve outcomes for older individuals with cancer. We must also understand the broader effect of the aged TME on the differentiation and function of CD8+ T cells. Here, we show that aging compromises tumor control by intrinsically impairing the persistence and proliferation of antigen-specific CD8+ T cells. The aged TME induces a novel and evolutionarily conserved state of age-associated dysfunction, distinct from CD8+ T cell exhaustion, even within transferred young CD8+ T cells. Broader shifts in the immune landscape in aged tumors erode natural killer (NK) cell–dendritic cell (DC)–CD8+ T cell cross-talk and ultimately reduce CD8+ T cell priming by conventional type 1 DCs (cDC1s). Due to these defects, aged tumor-bearing mice are unable to benefit from therapeutic mRNA vaccination. Finally, we show that myeloid-targeted immunotherapies that reinvigorate cDC1s can improve tumor control and enhance CD8+ T cell immunity in aged mice.

## Results

### Aging promotes tumor growth and alters CD8+ T cell fate and function

Aging is a cumulative process with no consensus on the exact onset of age-related immune dysfunction. We therefore started by profiling known features of T cell aging in mice, such as a relative decline in naive T cells5 and an increase in PD-1+TIM-3+CD8+ T cells over time17. These phenotypic changes sharply increased between 65 and 75 weeks in mice (Extended Data Fig. 1a), equivalent to 50- to 58-year-old humans18. Notably, this is approximately equivalent to the median age of cancer diagnosis in humans19. Thus, we implanted 1 × 106 ovalbumin (OVA)-expressing B16 melanoma (B16-OVA) cells in C57BL/6J mice aged between 10 and 68 weeks. Progressive aging was associated with significantly increased tumor growth (Fig. 1a). Next, we implanted B16-OVA melanoma cells or OVA-expressing Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC-OVA) cells into young (10–12 weeks) and aged (68–70 weeks) mice. Tumor growth was faster in the aged cohort 12–15 days after inoculation using both cell lines (Fig. 1b) and was coupled with fewer tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1b). We also observed reduced numbers of OVA-specific CD8+ T cells in aged mice within both the tumor and the tumor-draining lymph node (tdLN; Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1b,c).

To define heterogeneity within tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells, we next performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on over 5,000 CD8+ T cells from young and aged tumors (Fig. 1d) and used cell hashing to separate biological replicates (Extended Data Fig. 1d-f). As previously shown3,11,20,21, exhausted CD8+ T cells within the tumor uniformly expressed Pdcd1 (PD-1) and the transcription factor (TF) Tox. Within this population, we recovered the expected subsets of progenitor-like exhausted CD8+ T (TProg) cells, marked by Tcf7 (Tcf1)/Slamf6 expression, as well as terminally exhausted T (TTerm) cells marked by Havcr2 (TIM-3)/Entpd1 (CD39) expression (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 1g,h). However, both subsets of exhausted T cells were significantly depleted within the aged TME in favor of less differentiated T cell states, including naive-like (TNaiv), memory-like (TMem-like) and transitory (TTran) CD8+ T cells (Fig. 1e). We also identified a unique cluster of PD-1+Tox+IL-7R+CD8+ T cells enriched in aged tumors that did not express Tcf7, Slamf6 or Havcr2 (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 1g,h). To our knowledge, this cell state has not previously been characterized, and we hypothesized that this might be a unique tumor-infiltrating and age-associated dysfunctional subset of CD8+ T cells, termed TTAD cells.

We orthogonally validated our scRNA-seq findings using flow cytometry (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1b) and were able to readily identify TProg cells (SLAMF6+TIM-3−), TTran cells (SLAMF6+TIM-3+), TTerm cells (SLAMF6−TIM-3+) and the newly defined TTAD cells (SLAMF6−TIM-3−). The aged TME promoted TTAD cell formation within both B16-OVA melanoma and LLC-OVA lung carcinoma models (Fig. 1f,g), including within OVA-specific CD8+ T cells in the aged TME (Extended Data Fig. 1i). We noted a concordant decrease in the frequency of TTerm cells, which was further exacerbated in an older cohort of 90-week-old mice (Fig. 1f,g).

To assess if aging also impacts the effector capacity of tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cell responses, we used ex vivo restimulation assays to measure effector cytokine production. Our data showed significant decreases in interferon-γ (IFNγ), tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and interleukin-2 (IL-2) production within aged tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells (Fig. 1h). Next, we assessed cytotoxic potential via ex vivo granzyme B (GZMB) expression, which was reduced within all activated CD8+ T cell subsets in aged tumors (Fig. 1h). Finally, we defined the proliferative capacity of tumor-infiltrating T cells in vivo by measuring BrdU incorporation. The frequency of BrdU+ dividing CD8+ T cells was lower within aged tumors (Fig. 1h). Of note, age-associated functional defects could be observed across multiple CD8+ T cell subsets (Extended Data Fig. 1j). Together, these data suggest that aging impairs tumor control and broadly alters CD8+ T cell fate and function.

### T cell-intrinsic defects in aging lead to terminal differentiation

We wondered whether the age-associated changes observed within tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells could be solely explained by baseline T cell-intrinsic defects within healthy aged mice22. We reasoned that the transfer of aged CD8+ T cells into young tumor-bearing mice would clearly delineate cell-autonomous defects from those driven by additional signals within the aged TME. We thus co-transferred congenically marked CD45.1/CD45.2 young OT-1 (OT-1Y>Y) and CD45.1 aged OT-1 (OT-1A>Y) CD8+ T cells into young wild-type (CD45.2) tumor-bearing mice and profiled tumor-infiltrating transferred T cells 15 days later by scRNA-seq (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 2a-c). Our analysis revealed three main subclusters, including known subsets of TProg and TTerm cells as defined by their unique gene signatures (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 2b,d). We saw that aged OT-1A>Y T cells had a much higher ratio of TTerm cells to TProg cells than OT-1Y>Y T cells (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 2e). Aged OT-1A>Y TTerm cells also expressed less Ikzf2, consistent with prior reports23, and had higher expression of cell cycle inhibitors, such as Cdkn1a and Cdkn2a (Fig. 2d). This suggests that CD8+ T cell dysfunction in aging is at least partially intrinsically imprinted within CD8+ T cells.

To determine whether the high ratio of TTerm cells to TProg cells in aged OT-1A>Y mice (Fig. 2b,c) is due to cell-intrinsic defects in TProg cell formation or maintenance in the TME, we enumerated subset frequencies during early tumor progression (Fig. 2e). There were fewer TProg cells within OT-1A>Y mice than within OT-1Y>Y mice even as early as day 7 (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 2f). This suggests that aged OT-1 cells have a reduced ability to form TProg cells during the earliest phases of T cell infiltration into tumors. Moreover, the ratio of TTerm to TProg cells skewed further from day 9 to day 15 in the OT-1A>Y group. This suggests that, in addition to impaired TProg cell formation, cell-intrinsic changes within aged OT-1 cells also lead to poor maintenance of TProg cells, ultimately promoting premature terminal differentiation in the TME (Fig. 2f,g and Extended Data Fig. 2f).

We next wondered whether age-associated cell-intrinsic defects were already present at baseline before transfer. Comparison of young and aged splenic OT-1 CD8+ T cells before transfer revealed that aging expands antigen-experienced (CD44+PD-1+), but reduces naive (CD44−PD-1−), CD8+ T cell subsets, as previously observed5 (Extended Data Fig. 1a). TNaiv cells were also broadly altered in aging at the transcriptional level (Fig. 2h,i and Extended Data Fig. 2g-i). Critically, many of the transcriptional changes observed between young OT-1Y>Y and aged OT-1A>Y CD8+ T cells in the TME already existed within splenic CD8+ TNaiv cells at baseline, such as Ets1, Ikzf2, Il7r and Bcl2 (Fig. 2d,i,j). Despite lacking markers of antigen experience, such as PD-1 or CD44, OT-1 CD8+ TNaiv cells in aged versus young mice showed a global loss of naive-associated gene expression and relative enrichment of deletional tolerance or anergy-associated24 transcriptional programs (Fig. 2k).

Finally, we sought to understand how these changes would affect aged T cell function. Aged OT-1 CD8+ T cells showed diminished cytotoxicity in vitro at multiple effector-to-target ratios (Fig. 2l). To confirm cell-autonomous differences in tumor control, we then tested the ability of young and aged OT-1 CD8+ T cells to kill tumor cells in vivo. Consistent with the in vitro results, equal numbers of aged OT-1 CD8+ T cells transferred into young tumor-bearing mice (OT-1A>Y) failed to control B16-OVA tumor growth compared to their young counterparts (OT-1Y>Y; Fig. 2m). Taken together, these data suggest that aging leads to premature loss of naiveness/stemness at baseline. Furthermore, these cell-intrinsic defects are ultimately irreversible, promoting terminal differentiation of aged OT-1A>Y CD8+ T cells even within young tumor-bearing mice and contributing to poor tumor control in aging.

### Cell-intrinsic aging reduces proliferation but not the TTAD cell state

Our findings so far prompted the question: how are cell-intrinsic defects encoded within aged CD8+ TNaiv cells? Aging is known to have a profound impact on the epigenome6,25, and so we profiled chromatin accessibility changes within young and aged CD8+ T cells both at baseline (before transfer) and in the TME (after transfer; Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 3a). CD8+ TNaiv cells from aged mice showed increased accessibility at TF loci associated with T cell terminal differentiation, such as Id2 (refs. 26,27), and relative loss of naive/memory T cell-associated TFs such as Myb28,29 (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). Critically, differential expression of genes such as Ikzf2 and Bcl2 between young and aged OT-1A>Y TTerm cells in the TME could be explained by altered epigenetic regulation within aged naive splenocytes at baseline (Fig. 3b).

Further pathway analysis revealed that DNA damage/repair and replicative senescence signatures were differentially regulated in aged OT-1A>Y TTerm cells (Fig. 3c). These data suggest that, in addition to prematurely gaining features of terminal differentiation, aged CD8+ T cells might be intrinsically susceptible to genotoxic stress. To formally test this, we exposed young and aged CD8+ T cells to increasing amounts of DNA damage-inducing UV irradiation and measured relative upregulation of γH2AX (a known marker of DNA damage; Fig. 3d). Aged CD8+ T cells indeed upregulated γH2AX faster and to higher absolute levels than their young counterparts. We additionally noted higher expression of p21, which links DNA damage to cell cycle arrest, not just after irradiation but also at baseline, consistent with our prior hypothesis (Fig. 3d).

Given the previously observed loss of naive-like features and enrichment of DNA damage pathways, we hypothesized that aged CD8+ T cells would intrinsically lose proliferative capacity in tumors. To test this, we transferred young OT-1Y and aged OT-1A CD8+ T cells into young tumor-bearing recipients and assessed BrdU incorporation (Fig. 3e). Aged OT-1A>Y CD8+ T cells had lower proliferative capacity even within young tumors due to cell-autonomous changes. To further validate this as a solely cell-intrinsic defect, we also set up a cell-extrinsic paradigm where we transferred young OT-1Y>A CD8+ T cells into young and aged tumor-bearing mice. We observed equal amounts of BrdU incorporation in transferred young T cells, in marked contrast to the endogenous CD8+ T cells within the same aged TME (Fig. 3e).

We next wondered whether cell-autonomous defects in aging might also explain the accumulation of TTAD cells within the aged TME. We thus repeated our cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic transfer experiments and specifically assessed the frequency of TTAD cells in the TME. Surprisingly, we saw no evidence of the TTAD cell subset when aged OT-1A > Y cells were transferred into young tumor-bearing mice (Fig. 3f,g). This was associated with a concomitant loss of the TTerm cell subset within both endogenous and transferred young OT-1Y>A T cells in aged mice (Fig. 3f,g). Conversely, we readily identified TTAD cell formation not only within endogenous cells but also within transferred young OT-1Y>A CD8+ T cells in the aged TME (Fig. 3f,g). These data suggest that although cell-intrinsic defects in aging promote premature T cell differentiation and genotoxic stress, they do not drive the differentiation of the TTAD cell subset in the aged TME.

### Cell-extrinsic signals in the aged TME drive the TTAD cell state

Although we observed cell-autonomous changes in CD8+ T cell proliferation, our data also showed that the enrichment of TTAD cells in the aged TME (Fig. 1d-g) was not intrinsically imprinted within aged CD8+ T cells (Fig. 3f,g). This suggests that the formation of TTAD cells requires other signals within the aged tumor milieu. To investigate the impact of cell-extrinsic signaling within the aged TME, we transferred young CD45.1+ splenic OT-1Y CD8+ T cells into young (OT-1Y>Y) and aged (OT-1Y>A) CD45.2+ B16-OVA tumor-bearing mice (Fig. 4a). We found that the transfer of young antigen-specific OT-1 CD8+ T cells was not sufficient to rescue impaired tumor control in aged mice (Fig. 4a), suggesting that the aged TME plays a critical role in limiting tumor control by CD8+ T cells. Consistent with this, we recovered fewer transferred tumor-infiltrating OT-1 CD8+ T cells from aged mice (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). Moreover, our data implied that tumor control by transferred OT-1 CD8+ T cells is significantly more impacted by cell-extrinsic signals from the aged TME than by cell-intrinsic changes from aging (Extended Data Fig. 4c). Thus, we hypothesized that the aged TME not only drives the differentiation of a distinct TTAD cell subset that is specifically induced by cell-extrinsic signals in the aged TME but also limits CD8+ T cell priming and expansion, which is associated with poor tumor control.

We next wanted to understand the functional properties of this new TTAD cell subset in the aged TME. Compared to TTerm cells from the same aged tumors, TTAD cells expressed similar amounts of IFNγ and IL-2 but had increased TNF production (Fig. 4b). Conversely, the cytotoxic molecule GZMB was significantly reduced in TTAD cells. We also noted increased levels of γH2AX within TTAD cells compared to in TTerm cells from young and aged tumors (Fig. 4b).

To further assess the direct cytotoxic capacity of TTAD cells, we isolated intratumoral OVA-tetramer+CD8+ (Tet+CD8+) T cell subsets, including endogenous TProg, TTerm and TTAD cells, from both young and aged tumors and cocultured them with B16-OVA cells (Extended Data Fig. 4d). As expected, both young and aged TProg cells exhibited similar low cytotoxicity levels (approximately 5–10%)11. Young TTerm cells showed slightly higher cytotoxicity (approximately 15–20%) in killing tumor cells than aged TTerm cells (approximately 5–15%). Notably, TTAD cells showed almost no cytotoxicity (around 5%; Extended Data Fig. 4d). To further confirm the impact of cell-extrinsic signals in driving poor cytotoxicity within TTAD cells, we repeated the same in vitro cytotoxicity assay with subsets of transferred young OT-1 CD8+ T cells isolated from young and aged tumors and observed similar results. Critically, OT-1 TTAD cells also exhibited lower cytotoxicity (around 5%), similar to Tet+ TTAD cells (Fig. 4c). Finally, we assessed the impact on in vivo tumor control by transferring different isolated Tet+CD45.2+CD8+ T cell subsets into young CD45.1+CD45.2+ tumor-bearing mice on day 2 after inoculation. After 8 days, only mice that received young TProg cells demonstrated better tumor control, whereas mice did not benefit in any way from receiving TTAD cells (Fig. 4d). These results imply that aged mice with a higher proportion of TTAD cells in their tumors experience worse tumor control due to their poor cytotoxicity. This functional profile is notably distinct from canonical CD8+ T cell exhaustion in tumors, which is associated with broad decreases in effector cytokine production along with relative preservation of cytotoxicity11,30.

To orthogonally validate this, we defined the transcriptional state of transferred TTAD cells relative to all other transferred OT-1 CD8+ T cell subsets within the aged TME. First, we confirmed that scRNA-seq profiling of transferred OT-1Y>Y and OT-1Y>A T cells also showed a bias away from TTerm cells and toward TTAD cell formation in aged mice (Fig. 4e,f and Extended Data Fig. 5a-c). Comparison of TTAD cells and TTerm cells pinpointed distinct gene expression patterns within TTAD cells, including high expression of Il7r, Emb, Zfp36l2 and Fos (Extended Data Fig. 5d). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) confirmed the transcriptional similarity between transferred OT-1 CD8+ T cells (TTerm and TTAD cells) and the corresponding endogenous populations (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 5d). GSEA further highlighted that metabolism/cell cycle-associated genes were depleted in TTAD cells, whereas senescence31 and TNF signaling pathways were enriched relative to in TTerm cells (Fig. 4g). These data are also consistent with increased levels of γH2AX and TNF previously observed within TTAD cells (Fig. 4b). Thus, TTAD cells are a phenotypically and transcriptionally distinct subpopulation of tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells that are specifically elicited by cell-extrinsic signals in the aged TME.

We next conducted in vivo fate mapping transfer assays to understand the differentiation potential of TTAD cells and the lineage relationship between TTAD cells and other exhausted T cell subsets in the tumor11. Intratumoral Tet+CD8+ T cell subsets, including TProg, TTerm and TTAD cells, from both young and aged tumors were intravenously transferred into young tumor-bearing mice (Extended Data Fig. 4e). After an 8-day period in the tumor, both transferred young and aged TProg cells could differentiate into TTran cells and eventually reach the TTerm cell state, as expected11. Similarly, both young and aged TTerm cells remained in the TTerm cell state, indicative of terminal differentiation/exhaustion. Notably, we discovered that TTAD cells could partially differentiate into TTerm cells when reintroduced into the young host, suggesting that cell-extrinsic environmental factors might be critical for both TTAD cell formation and maintenance (Extended Data Fig. 4f,g).

Previous studies have identified different degrees of overlap between age-related changes and CD8+ T cell exhaustion17. Our group has previously defined a core epigenetic signature that can act as a precise biomarker of the exhausted state11,32. Although this core program strongly overlapped with the chromatin accessibility profile of TTerm cells, TTAD cells failed to enrich for this signature (Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 5f). The epigenetic landscape of TTAD cells also failed to enrich for memory and effector CD8+ T cell programs (Fig. 4h), consistent with the lowered GZMB expression within this subset (Fig. 4b).

We next sought to better understand the regulation of TTAD cells in the aged TME. Characterization of superenhancers and their associated genes has become a leading strategy to define important regulatory nodes in many cell types33,34. Therefore, we leveraged an algorithm that we have previously developed to infer superenhancer-associated genes within TTerm and TTAD cells32. Superenhancer-associated genes within TTerm cells included known drivers of CD8+ T cell exhaustion, such as Prdm1 (ref. 35), Bhlhle40 (ref. 36) and Maf37 (Fig. 4i). By contrast, top superenhancer-associated genes within TTAD cells did not clearly map onto known CD8+ T cell states, such as exhaustion, memory or effector (Fig. 4i). These included genes such as Zfp36l1 (refs. 38,39), Klf3 (refs. 40,41) and Fam49b42, which are thought to limit expansion and effector function in CD8+ T cells, and previously uncharacterized genes such as Gm21811 (Fig. 4i). Moreover, using the scRNA-seq SCENIC package, we also identified different and key transcriptional factors (for example, Ets1, Junb and Maf) that were active in TTAD cells compared to in TProg and TTerm cells (Extended Data Fig. 5e). These data suggest that TTAD cells are not simply ‘hyperexhausted’ but represent a unique state of CD8+ T cells in the aged TME that lacks effector functions.

Finally, we wondered whether similar TTAD cells could be identified in human cancer. Reanalysis of human tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells from published pan-cancer scRNA-seq datasets43-45 identified an analogous cluster of PD-1+IL-7R+CD8+ T cells that did not express SLAMF6 and TIM-3 (Fig. 4j and Extended Data Fig. 5g-i). Critically, this cluster was enriched in tumor biopsies from older (60–90 years old), but not younger (40–59 years old), individuals (Fig. 4k). Supporting our expectation, cells falling within the human TTAD cell cluster showed strong enrichment for the mouse TTAD cell transcriptional signature (Fig. 4l). This included specific upregulation of human TTAD cell-associated genes, such as FOS, FOSB, DUSP1 and IL7R (Extended Data Fig. 5h,i). Taken together, our data suggest that TTAD cells represent a cell lineage with reduced effector capacity that is distinct from T cell exhaustion and is also expanded within the tumors of older individuals with cancer. Furthermore, we show that the trajectory of CD8+ T cell differentiation in general and the formation of TTAD cells in particular are almost entirely driven by cell-extrinsic signals in the aged TME.

### The aged TME erodes immune cell cross-talk, impairing T cell responses

Our data thus far indicate that cell-extrinsic signals in the aged TME outweigh CD8+ T cell-intrinsic defects in tumor control. This prompted us to ask: what mechanisms limit CD8+ T cell antitumor immunity within the aged TME? We started by enumerating important immune populations within young and aged tumors using flow cytometry in both B16-OVA melanoma and LLC-OVA lung carcinoma models (Fig. 5a,b and Extended Data Fig. 6a). Only CD8+ T cell, NK cell and DC frequencies were consistently and significantly lower in aged tumors (Fig. 5b).

Based on these data, we hypothesized that impaired NK cell–DC–CD8+ T cell cross-talk in the aged TME might underlie poor CD8+ T cell priming and expansion. We therefore investigated the effects of aging on tumor-infiltrating immune cell state and cross-talk more broadly using scRNA-seq profiling (Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 6b). The aged TME had globally lower levels of antigen presentation genes, such as Psme1, Psme2, Tap1 and B2m, as well as decreased expression of key chemokines for immune cell recruitment, such as Xcl1, Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 (Extended Data Fig. 6c). We found that these aged DCs did downregulate the expression of molecules related to antigen presentation (B2m and Tap1) and upregulated the expression of Apoe, which can inhibit antigen presentation46 (Fig. 5d). Moreover, our analysis suggested that tumors in aged mice specifically had fewer interactions between NK cells, cDC1s and CD8+ T cells (Fig. 5e). Indeed, we noted that NK cells provided increased supportive signaling to cDC1s through both the Flt3l–Flt3 and Xcl1–Xcr1 axes in young, but not in aged, tumors. Conversely, cDC1s and NK cells had stronger interactions through the Clec2d–Klrb1b axis in the aged TME, which likely inhibits NK cell function (Extended Data Fig. 6d). These data help explain the reduced frequencies of NK cells and DCs in the aged TME as observed by flow cytometry (Fig. 5b). We next focused on interactions between CD8+ T cells and cDC1s, which are needed for optimal priming and reactivation of CD8+ T cells47,48. Young tumors not only had stronger major histocompatibility complex class I–T cell antigen receptor (MHC class I–TCR) interactions between cDC1s and CD8+ T cells but also had higher levels of CD8-derived CXCL10 and IFNγ, which promote antitumor immune cell recruitment.

Because XCL1 secretion by NK cells is critical for cDC1 recruitment and differentiation49, we wondered if cDC1 populations were altered in aged mice within the TME. To assess this, we implanted B16-OVA cells in C57BL/6J mice of different ages, ranging from 10 to 68 weeks. Consistent with our prior data, our studies revealed that age progressively promoted tumor growth while diminishing the proportion of intratumoral CD8+ T cells, Tet+CD8+ T cells and TTerm cells, as well as increasing TTAD cells (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 6e,f). Concurrently, progressive aging led to a decline in the frequencies of cDC1s and a concomitant reduction in CD40, CD86, MHC class I/MHC class II and FLT3 levels in cDC1s (Fig. 5f,g). These results suggest that the decrease in cDC1s and their diminished antigen presentation capacity may constrain TTerm cell formation and facilitate TTAD cell formation. Moreover, the reduction in cDC1s was found not only in the tumor but also in the tdLN and non-draining LN (Fig. 5h,i). This is consistent with our prior data showing reduced priming of Tet+CD8+ T cells in aged tumor-bearing mice (Fig. 1c). Taken together, these data suggest that the aged TME lacks a key amplifying feedforward loop present in young tumors where NK cell-derived XCL1 draws in cDC1s to activate large numbers of CD8+ T cells (Fig. 5j), which in turn release inflammatory cytokines to recruit more immune cells.

### Myeloid-targeted therapy rescues poor T cell priming by aged cDC1s

T cell–cDC1 interactions are also a critical determinant of immunotherapy outcomes47,48,50. We thus wondered if aged tumor-bearing mice would have impaired responses to mRNA neoantigen vaccines, which are currently being investigated in multiple cancer types. To test this, we optimized an OVA-mRNA delivery system using lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Young tumor-bearing mice that received OVA-mRNA LNPs as a therapeutic vaccine had better tumor control than nonvaccinated mice (Fig. 6a,b). By contrast, aged tumor-bearing mice showed no benefit from receiving OVA-mRNA-based vaccines (Fig. 6a,b). OVA-mRNA vaccination was associated with increased numbers of CD8+ T cells in the tumors and tdLNs of young, but not aged, mice (Fig. 6c). These data suggest that lack of local guidance from cDC1s in aged LNs and tumors impairs vaccine immunotherapy responses.

CD40 agonists are known to increase myeloid cell numbers and function in tumors48,51,52. We therefore wondered if reinvigorating cDC1 populations in the aged TME through CD40 agonism could rescue CD8+ T cell immunity. Compared to nontreated controls, young tumor-bearing mice that received CD40 agonist treatment had better tumor control (Fig. 6d,e) with increased cDC1s and CD8+ T cells in the tdLN (Fig. 6f). Critically, tumor control in aged mice was also significantly improved after CD40 agonist treatment (Fig. 6d, e), with increased frequencies of cDC1s found specifically in the tdLNs (Fig. 6f). Consistent with our hypothesis, this was also associated with increased expansion of CD8+ T cells in the tumor and the tdLN (Fig. 6f). It is worth noting that reinvigorating myeloid cells through CD40 agonism in aged mice leads to similar tumor control as seen at baseline in young tumor-bearing mice (Fig. 6e). We also observed increased levels of CD40, CD86, MHC class I/MHC class II and FLT3 in aged cDC1s comparable to the levels observed in young cDC1s after treatment, indicating that the CD40 agonist has the potential to rescue cDC1 antigen presentation and cross-talk with CD8+ T cells (Fig. 6g).

To further characterize the impact of CD40 agonist treatment, we conducted scRNA-seq (Fig. 6h and Extended Data Fig. 7). We observed that subsets of exhausted CD8+ T cells (for example, TProg and TTerm cells) decreased, whereas the TMem-like and effector-like (TEff-like) cell subsets increased after treatment (Fig. 6i,j). Notably, we observed a reduction in the TTAD cell subset after CD40 agonist treatment. Taken together, we show that restoring cDC1 numbers through myeloid-targeted immunotherapies in aged tumor-bearing mice can enhance CD8+ T cell priming/expansion, prevent TTAD cell formation and ultimately improve tumor control.

## Discussion

Improving cancer immunotherapy outcomes in older individuals will require the identification of mechanisms limiting CD8+ T cell immunity in the aged TME as well as new strategies for reinvigorating dysfunctional CD8+ T cells. Here, we have taken a multipronged and systematic approach to evaluating the mechanisms driving age-associated CD8+ T cell dysfunction. We show that aging impairs tumor control and reduces CD8+ T cell infiltration and function. This inhibition is partially mediated by cell-extrinsic factors in the aged TME, because transferred young antigen-specific CD8+ T cells fail to persist and control tumor growth in aged mice. We identify a previously unknown subset of dysfunctional CD8+ T cells specifically associated with an aged TME (TTAD cells), which are functionally, transcriptionally and epigenetically distinct from canonical exhausted CD8+ T cells, in mouse and human tumors. Finally, we show that aging reduces the infiltration of NK cells and cDC1s, which are critical for initiating robust CD8+ T cell responses, ultimately preventing aged mice from responding to mRNA neoantigen vaccines.

Our study has several key implications. Previous studies have found that the persistence and immunotherapy responses of tumor-infiltrating CD8+ cells are reduced in aging53-56. However, other contemporaneous studies also suggested that aged mice control tumor growth better than young mice in some contexts57,58. First, our study helps resolve this contradiction by disentangling the T cell-intrinsic versus T cell-extrinsic effects of aging on CD8+ T cell function in cancer. We show that aged CD8+ T cells are intrinsically limited in their proliferative capacity and uniquely vulnerable to genotoxic stress, predisposing them to terminal exhaustion in tumors. Conversely, altered signals from the aged TME independently shape the differentiation of CD8+ T cells, diverting them away from canonical T cell exhaustion. Thus, the ultimate outcome of aging on CD8+ T cell-mediated antitumor immunity in a specific context will depend on the relative contribution of these counterbalancing cell-intrinsic versus extrinsic effects.

Second, we establish a potential new paradigm to explain tumor progression and immunotherapy resistance, specifically the presence of a distinct age-associated TTAD cell subset. TTAD cells were transcriptionally and epigenetically distinct from canonical exhausted CD8+ T cells and maintained little to no effector function. Critically, we show that this senescence-like cell fate could be induced by cell-extrinsic signals from the aged TME even within transferred young CD8+ T cells. Aged CD8+ T cells are thus not simply ‘hyperexhausted’ but represent a distinct CD8+ T cell lineage likely driven by impaired DC–CD8+ T cell cross-talk in the aged TME. We were able to translate our findings from mouse models to humans to show a pan-cancer increase in TTAD cells within older individuals. Open questions remain on whether TTAD cells would also be found in more engineered T cell contexts, such as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells, that are less dependent on physiological in vivo priming from DCs. Indeed, age-related dysfunction may help explain results from recent phase 2/phase 3 B cell maturation antigen-targeted CAR T cell therapy trials in multiple myeloma where almost all individuals relapsed after initial response59,60. Further work to understand the impact of TTAD cells will be essential not just in cancer but also in other diseases where the role of T cell aging is being investigated61,62.

Finally, we show that defects within CD8+ T cells and cDC1s in the aged TME restrict the ability of aged mice to respond to mRNA vaccines. Despite promising early results in humans63, our preclinical data suggest that older individuals with cancer may have reduced benefit from this immunotherapy strategy due to the inability of CD8+ T cells to be adequately primed by aged cDC1s. This would also be consistent with real-world outcomes seen with the COVID mRNA vaccine, where older individuals had attenuated immune responses and reduced clinical protection64,65. We also show that myeloid-targeted immunotherapies, such as CD40 agonism, can rescue age-associated defects in CD8+ T cell immunity and tumor control. Therefore, targeted adjuvant(s) to recruit more cDC1 into tumors, facilitate CD8+ T cell priming and/or boost CD8+ T cell function may be required to improve cancer immunotherapy responses and outcomes in older individuals with cancer.

## Methods

### Mice

Female C57BL/6J mice (strain 000664), CD45.1 congenic mice (B6.SJL-PtprcaPepcb/BoyJ, strain 002014) and OT-1 transgenic mice (strain C57BL/6-Tg(TcraTcrb) 1100 Mjb/J) were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory. OT-1 transgenic mice were bred with CD45.1 congenic mice and were crossed to generate OT-1 CD45.1 mice for in vivo adoptive transfer and in vitro coculture experiments. Some aged OT-1 mice were a gift from T. Mempel (Massachusetts General Hospital). All breeding mice and subsequent litters were genotyped at Transnetyx. Tumor sizes on all tumor-bearing mice were not >20 mm, as the maximum permitted tumor size. All experimental mice were housed under specific pathogen-free conditions and used in accordance with ethical regulations and were preapproved by the Massachusetts General Hospital Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

### Cell lines and tumor inoculation

B16-OVA and LLC-OVA cells modified to express OVA were gifts from B. Miller (University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill) and R. Manguso (Broad Institute), respectively. Cells were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin and maintained at 37 °C with 5% CO2. Cells underwent intermittent mycoplasma testing using a LookOut Mycoplasma PCR detection kit (Sigma). Mice were subcutaneously injected with 1 × 106 B16-OVA cells or 1 × 106 LLC-OVA cells in 1× HBSS (Life Technologies). Tumors were measured every 3 days starting at day 6 after tumor injection. Tumor volume (mm3) was calculated using the following formula: V = L × W × W/2, where L and W denotes length and width, respectively.

### CD8+ T cell isolation from tissues

On the indicated days after tumor cell injection, tumors were dissected from the surrounding fascia, mechanically minced and treated with collagenase P (2 mg ml−1; Sigma) and DNase I (50 μg ml−1; Sigma) for 15 min at 37 °C. After tumor samples were filtered with a 70-μm filter, tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes were first isolated using a Percoll gradient composed of 35% (vol/vol) and 65% (vol/vol) Percoll (Cytiva). The lymphocyte-containing phase was further enriched by CD45+ or CD8b+ MACS+ selection (Miltenyi). When necessary, cells were sorted on a FACSAria II (BD Biosciences) for downstream scRNA-seq and/or ATAC-seq analyses. Spleens and LNs were dissected, mechanically minced and filtered into single-cell suspensions. Red blood cell lysis (RBC lysis buffer, Biolegend) was performed on all spleen samples, with subsequent CD8+ T cell MACS+ selection (Miltenyi).

### Isolation of splenic CD8+ T cells for adoptive T cell transfer

To prepare OT-1 CD8+ T cells for co-transfer and single-transfer experiments, spleens were dissected from age- and sex-matched CD45.1+ (or CD45.1+CD45.2+) OT-1 mice, mechanically minced and filtered to a single-cell suspension. Red blood cell lysis (RBC lysis buffer, Biolegend) was subsequently performed on spleen samples, followed by mouse CD8a+ MACS untouched isolation kit (Miltenyi). An aliquot of splenic CD8+ T cells was stained with Live/Dead, CD8Bb.2, TCR Vβ5.1, TCR Vβ5.2, CD45.1 and CD45.2 to assess CD8+ T cell purity and to verify OT-1 and CD45.1+CD45.2+ expression. In total, 5,000 OT-1 CD8+ T cells expressing the desired congenic marker were suspended in RPMI (Gibco) containing 1% FBS and intravenously injected into recipient mice 1 day before tumor inoculation. For the relevant cell-intrinsic experiments in Fig. 2, CD45.1+CD45.2+ young and CD45.1+ aged OT-1 CD8+ T cells (as donor cells) were isolated from spleens and mixed at a 1:1 ratio for a total transfer dose of 5,000 cells per recipient mouse.

### Flow cytometry and antibodies

To investigate phenotypic and functional changes by flow cytometry, cells were blocked with anti-mouse CD16/CD32 (Biolegend) and surface stained with the indicated antibodies (Supplementary Table 1) for 20 min at 4 °C. NIR Live/Dead (1:1,000; Thermo Fisher Scientific) dye, used to exclude dead cells from downstream flow cytometry analysis, was added in parallel with surface antibodies. To investigate intracellular markers, cells were fixed and permeabilized using a Foxp3/Transcription Factor Staining Buffer set (eBiosciences), as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Cells were blocked again with 5% mouse and rat serum plus anti-mouse CD16/CD32 and stained with intracellular antibodies for 30 min at 4 °C.

For BrdU experiments, mice were administered 1 mg of BrdU (BD Pharmigen) via intraperitoneal injection 14–16 h before tissue collection. BrdU staining was performed after cell-surface staining, as per the manufacturer’s protocol.

For UV radiation experiments, spleens were collected from female C57BL/6J mice in the indicated age ranges, filtered into single-cell suspensions and enriched for CD8+ T cells using a CD8a+ T cell Isolation kit (Miltenyi), as previously described. In total, 5 × 105 CD8+ T cells in each age range were plated into a 24-well plate where they were subsequently irradiated with UV-C (~254 nm; 3,000 cGy) for 0, 1, 2 or 3 h. These cells were then collected and prepared for flow cytometry by staining cells with a live/dead stain as well as cell-surface markers (CD8b, TIM-3, CD44, PD-1 and SLAMF6) described in Supplementary Table 18 for 20 min at 4 °C. Cells were then fixed and permeabilized using a Foxp3/Transcription Factor Staining Buffer set (eBiosciences), as per the manufacturer’s instructions. After permeabilization, cells were stained overnight with p21 (Supplementary Table 18) for 30 min at 4 °C and subsequently stained with anti-IgG1 conjugated to PerCP-Cy5.5 (Supplementary Table 18) for 30 min at 4 °C. Last, γH2AX (Supplementary Table 18) was stained for 2 h at 4 °C before flow cytometry analyses.

A BD Fortessa X-20 (BD Biosciences) flow cytometer and FACSDiva software (v.8.0.1, BD Pharmingen) were used to collect data, and analyses were performed using FlowJo software (v.10.9.0, BD). Single-color compensation controls and fluorescence minus one thresholds were used to set flow gate margins.

### In vitro cytokine production and cytotoxicity assays

To assess in vitro cytokine production of splenic-derived CD8+ T cells, 2 × 105 cells were activated in a flat 96-well plate coated with 1 μg ml−1 anti-CD3 (Fisher Scientific) and 1 μg ml−1 anti-CD28 (Fisher Scientific) in complete RPMI with 100 U ml−1 recombinant human IL-2. Forty-eight hours after activation, cells were treated with cell stimulation reagent (PMA/ionomycin plus protein inhibitors (eBiosciences)) for 4 h. The cells were stained for surface antigens, fixed, permeabilized and stained for IFNγ, TNF and IL-2 using a BD Cytofix/Cytoperm Fixation/Permeabilization kit, as per the manufacturer’s instructions.

To evaluate direct cytotoxicity, we performed an in vitro killing assay. B16-OVA cells were maintained under the same conditions as described in ‘Cell lines and tumor inoculation’ and served as targets, while OT-1 CD8+ T cells served as effectors. Specifically, splenic OT-1 CD8+ T cells from young mice (8–12 weeks) and aged mice (>64 weeks) were isolated and enriched as previously described and were maintained in RPMI 1640 supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco), 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Life Technologies), 1% l-glutamine (Life Technologies), 1% HEPES (Gibco) and 0.1% β-mercaptoethanol (Sigma) for 48 h at a concentration of 5 × 105 cells per well in a 96-well flat-bottom plate coated with 1 μg ml−1 anti-CD3 (Fisher Scientific) and 1 μg ml−1 anti-CD28 (Fisher Scientific). B16-OVA cells were treated with IFNγ (100 ng ml−1; PeproTech) overnight before setting up the killing assay to upregulate MHC class I. On the day of the killing assay, IFNγ-treated B16-OVA cells were washed with 1× DPBS−/−, labeled with 0.1 μM Cell Trace Violet (Fisher Scientific) and plated at 5,000 B16-OVA cells per well. Tumor cells were incubated for 4 h at 37 °C and 5% CO2 for cells to adhere to the plate. Different amounts of T cells were then added in accordance with specific effector:target ratios (1:8, 1:4, 1:2, 1:1, 2:1, 4:1 and 8:1). After 72 h of coculture, the cells were trypsinized, stained and analyzed by flow cytometry to assess the number of remaining live tumor cells. Percent (%) cytotoxicity was calculated by using the following formula: 100% ×[1 − (number of live tumor cells in well with T cells/number of live tumor cells in well with no T cells)].

### Preparation of OVA-mRNA LNPs and CD40 agonistic antibody

LNPs containing OVA-mRNA were prepared as previously described66,67. Briefly, for every five mice, we prepared 125 μl of the ethanol phase by combining C12-200 (BroadPharm, BP-26474), 18:0 PC (DSPC; Avanti Polar Lipids, 850365C-200mg), cholesterol (Sigma, C8667-5G) and DMG-PEG 2000 (Avanti Polar Lipids, 880151P-1G) at a molar ratio of 35:16:46.5:2.5. We next prepared 375 μl of the aqueous phase by mixing 287.5 μl of nuclease-free water (Invitrogen), 37.5 μl of 0.1 M citrate buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 50 μl of CleanCap OVA-mRNA (TriLink; 1.0 mg ml−1 in 1 mM sodium citrate, pH 6.4). The ethanol and aqueous phases were mixed at a 1:3 ratio. We next dialyzed the LNPs against DPBS−/− (Gibco) by using an Amicon Ultra Centrifugal Filter unit (Sigma, UFC8100), adding our mixed sample into the device and centrifuging at 4,000g for 30 min at room temperature. We then added 10 ml of exchange buffer (that is, DPBS−/−) to the Amicon unit and repeated the centrifugation step. Last, we resuspended the LNPs containing OVA-mRNA in 500 μl of 1× DPBS−/− (Gibco) to achieve a final concentration 100 μg ml−1 OVA-mRNA. On day 6 after tumor inoculation, the mice were subcutaneously injected with 100 μl of LNPs containing 10 μg of OVA-mRNA. Furthermore, in CD40 agonistic antibody-treated groups, on days 2 and 7, the mice were intraperitoneally injected with 100 μg of anti-CD40 (clone FGK4.5, BioXCell) or 100 μg of isotype-matched control antibody.

### scRNA-seq library preparation and analysis

Live tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells (or OT-1 CD8+ T cells) and/or intratumoral CD45+ cells were sorted from tumors on day 15 after tumor inoculation by a BD FACSSymphony S6 Sorter (BD). Sorted cells were pooled into groups (five biological replicates per group), with independent mice being labeled with TotalSeq-B Hashtags (Biolegend). Cells were counted and loaded onto the Chromium Controller (10x Genomics) for a target recovery of 10,000 single cells per run. Samples were then processed using a 10x Single Cell 3′ v3.1 kit, as per the manufacturer’s protocol. Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq S2 or NextSeq 1000/2000 sequencer using 100-cycle kits with paired-end reads.

The CellRanger analysis pipeline (v.6.1.1) was used to perform sample demultiplexing, barcode processing, alignment, filtering, unique molecular identifier counting and aggregation of sequencing runs. Transcripts were aligned to the mm10 transcriptome (CellRanger version 2020-A). Downstream analyses were performed in R (v.4.2.1) using the Seurat package (v.4.3.0). In downstream analysis, cells with fewer than 200 unique genes, greater than 3,500 unique genes and greater than 10% mitochondrial reads were removed, yielding, on average, an expression matrix of ~6,000 cells by ~15,000 genes. Gene expression measurements were normalized by total expression per cell, multiplied by a scaling factor of 10,000 and transformed using log (1p). The top 3,000 most variable features were selected using the ‘vst’ method in Seurat’s FindVariableFeatures for PCA analysis. The top PCs were calculated and determined to be significant (P<0.01) using the ‘elbow plot’ method. A UMAP was calculated from 15–20 PCs using default parameters. Unsupervised clustering was performed using the original Louvain algorithm. Multiple clustering resolutions were examined, and an optimal resolution of between 0.4 and 0.6 for clustering was selected for further analysis. All differential expression analysis was performed using DESeq2, and volcano plots were made using EnhancedVolcano (v.1.18.0). Fast preranked GSEA was performed on differentially expressed genes using fgsea (v.1.26.0). All gene sets from the Hallmarks (50 gene sets), C2 (6,290 gene sets), C5 (15,937 gene sets) and C7 (5,219 gene sets) databases from MSigDB were tested, for a total of 27,496 gene sets. Visualizations were created with ggplot2 (v.3.4.2). Inference and analysis of cell–cell communication from total CD45+ scRNA-seq data were performed using CellChat (v.1.6.0) under default settings. TF regulatory network analysis was performed on scRNA-seq data using the R package single-cell regulatory network inference and clustering (SCENIC; v.1.3.1), with default settings. TF–gene coexpression modules were determined by matching targets with TFs within their top five regulators, resulting in 20 regulons. Average regulon activity was scored within cell-type clusters identified by Seurat.

The published human pan-cancer scRNA-seq datasets43-45 were collected from E-MTAB-8017, GSE115978 and GSE179994. Downstream analyses were performed in R (v.4.2.1) using the Seurat package (v.4.3.0). In downstream analysis, cells with fewer than 200 unique genes, greater than 5,900 unique genes and greater than 10% mitochondrial reads were removed and normalized by sctransform (v.0.3.5), and the CD8+ T cell cluster was purified, yielding, on average, an expression matrix of 7,242 CD8+ T cells by ~15,000 genes. Moreover, VISION (v3.0.1) was used to create an age-associated CD8+ T cell dysfunction gene signature library, and this library was used to predict the similarity between mouse and human age-associated CD8+ T cell clusters.

### ATAC-seq library preparation and analysis

Live tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells or OT-1 CD8+ T cells from tumors on day 15 after tumor inoculation were sorted and pooled into two or three independent biological replicates, which ranged from 5,000 to 50,000 cells per genotype/subset combination (TProg: SLAMF6+TIM-3−; TTerm: SLAMF6−TIM-3+; TTAD: SLAMF6−TIM-3−). As previously described68, pelleted cells were incubated in 5–50 μl of reaction mix containing 2× TD, Tn5 enzyme and 2% digitonin in nuclease-free water at 37 °C for 30 min with agitation at 1,000 rpm. A MinElute Reaction Cleanup kit (Qiagen) was used for DNA purification. Following PCR, bead cleanup was performed using AMPure XP beads (Beckman Coulter/Agencourt), library quality was verified using Tapestation analysis, and library quantification was confirmed by KAPA Library Quantification kit (Illumina Platforms; Roche). Sequencing was performed on a NextSeq 1000/2000 sequencer using paired-end 50-base pair reads.

Raw fastq files were downloaded from Illumina BaseSpace and merged across lanes. FastQC was run before and after trimming. Trim-momatic (v.0.36) was used for quality trimming and primer removal in raw fastq files with the following parameters: LEADING: 15, TRAILING: 15, SLIDINGWINDOW: 4:15, MINLEN: 30 and CROP: 35. Trimmed reads were aligned with Bowtie2 (v.2.2.9) to mm10, with a maximum insert size of 1,000 bases. Aligned bam files were sorted, and duplicates were marked (Picard v.2.8.0). Reads that mapped to the blacklist region were removed. MACS (v.2.1.1) was used to perform peak calling on merged bam files (Samtools v.1.3.1) from biological replicates using a q value threshold of 0.001. TDF files were generated using igvtools (v.2.3.98) for visualization using the Integrative Genomics Viewer (v.2.13.1, Broad Institute). Consensus peaks from all samples were merged to create a single peak universe. A raw counts matrix was generated for each biological replicate by quantifying the number of cut sites within each peak region. The ataqv package was used for data quality control, including transcription start site enrichment69. The Combat-seq method was used to batch correct samples sequenced at different time points by Surrogate Variable Analysis (sva, v.3.48.0), and peaks with fewer than 25 reads across all samples were removed. DESeq2 (v.1.40.2) was used for counts matrix normalization and for differential accessibility analysis between pairwise comparisons of all conditions. R (v.4.3.1) was used to perform PCA. Gene-to-peak associations were determined using the GREAT software package (v.3.0.0; http://bejerano.stanford.edu/great/public-3.0.0/html/) with default settings. GREAT was also used to determine the gene set enrichment, with default settings and hypergeometric and binomial tests to measure significance.

### Experimental design and statistical methods

Female mice were cohoused and randomized across cages before the start of the experiment to minimize cage-to-cage variation. Sample sizes of five to ten animals per experimental arm per experimental replicate were chosen to ensure adequate power. Data collection and analysis were not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments. Analyses were performed with GraphPad Prism 10 (version 10.0) or R. Unless otherwise stated, data are presented as mean ± s.d., and a two-tailed Student’s t-test was used. All tests were two sided unless otherwise specified. Significance was considered for P values of <0.05 (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01 and ***P < 0.001).
